utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good afternoon to you too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also good afternoon to the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel, Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and as usual good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon to my learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us today our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, Miss Adisa Mehic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. You may sit down. We'll be continuing with your testimony. I apologize to you for starting late, but we had a technical problem that we had to solve before we could continue. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, yesterday we got to the point where you had described General Morillon's failed escape attempt, shall we call it that, failed escape attempt. He didn't get very far, and the consternation that developed when you put him into your sleeping bag instead of his own and guards were running around looking for him. So you also mentioned yesterday that he had decided to diffuse the situation by announcing that he would not leave Srebrenica until certain things had occurred. That decision -- sorry, my question is: When did he make that decision to diffuse the situation by effectively saying, "Well, I will remain in captivity and refuse to leave until such time as other developments occurred"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon made that decision during the night whilst he was standing alone in that destroyed house alongside the road, watching the refugees come in. And the reason I say that is that when he came back in, the first time that Mihailov and I saw him again early in the morning, he said, "I'm going to stay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he decide that he would issue a speech announcing his decision?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he hadn't -- he didn't mention that at that stage. My concern was that the general was so tired and that he needed some -- some rest and he said, "We will discuss it when I get -- when I wake up."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think your evidence yesterday was that he managed to get some sleep and later in the morning, wake up, and can you please take up the narrative from that point. And I'm particularly interested in the speech, any speech that he may have decided to issue.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Morillon woke up, it was about 10.00 or so in the morning and he discussed with me what it was that he might do. He then met with members of the Srebrenica War Presidency and said to them that he would -- would stay. And in discussion with them it came up that he should make a declaration, which would be out loud to the refugees who were surrounding the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you and he proceed to draft a speech?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did the writing and he told me what he wanted to say and we discussed each section as we wrote it down, then I actually wrote it down. Meanwhile, the war committee were looking for a loudhailer, but in fact they didn't have one and the Canadian APC, for some strange reason, had a loudhailer in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to eventually settle upon a draft?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did General Morillon, in fact, deliver that speech?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He delivered it from the first floor window of the PTT -- the new PTT building. And it was -- General Morillon read out one -- it's in English, from the -- this notebook. And then the UNHCR translator, who was there from, I think it was from Belgrade, then translated that sentence into Serbo-Croat and General Morillon read out the next sentence and the translator --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you make various entries in your diary relating to the draft text of the speech?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wrote down the text as General Morillon dictated it. We would discuss a section, then he would dictate and I wrote, discuss a section, he'd dictate and I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But you made entries relating to the text of his speech and he was telling you what the text should be.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he dictating in English or was he dictating in French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were speaking in French and when it came to the exact words, then it was in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he made his speech or he read his speech from the diary in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, you are a fluent French speaker, are you not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And German and Dutch. MR. DI FAZIO: And German and Dutch. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to briefly show you a photograph, please, which is available to Your Honours on Sanction. Hard copies are available as well. Would you just take a look at that photograph, please. You have the photograph. Who is the man in the foreground with the UN flag?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may or may not be able to tell us, but have you any idea, could you venture an answer as to when that photograph might have been taken? On the day of the speech or on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That photograph was taken later on the same day of the speech. I went up with him, together with a couple of news reporters, journalists who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell Their Honours, what is that white building that you see directly across with a mound of dirt rising up to its doors?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Srebrenica hospital that I was referring to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I tender this photograph, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this would be 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P514, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this photograph, which I don't see an ERN number to it, is being tendered by the Prosecution and admitted and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P514. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to show you, Colonel Tucker, a short -- couple of short excerpts from a video, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, these are excerpts from Exhibit P432. Would Your Honours just bear with me. I just want to make I've got my exhibit number right. I was correct, it's portions from Exhibit P432.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, I just want you to look at the events that are being depicted. They're very brief excerpts. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please. In fact, could we go back a bit, please. Back to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, sir. [Cell phone ringing] MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Perhaps if we just play and get -- hold it there. I don't think there is any dispute, that's General Morillon, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day that we were prevented from leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So that's the, in effect, the day before?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And just play on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't see the face very well because of the writing, but who is the gentleman standing up there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Canadian sergeant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at this excerpt as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's being shown and the occasion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is when General Morillon read out the statement -- General Morillon on the right, just by the flag, and the person to the left is the UNHCR translator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the bull horn that you were talking about before.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. So you can see large numbers of people assembled on both occasions. Both when you were prevented from leaving and the following day when the general gave his message, read out his message having made his decision to stay. There were refugees milling all around the PTT building and the area where you were quartered, so to speak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, was it of significance to get the text of the message, this position that General Morillon had adopted, to the outside world as well as deliver it to the refugees and the populace of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was important. Firstly, there had been two journalists present who had recorded some of the footage that you saw. And we arranged for the videotapes that they had taken to be taken out of the enclave by UN military observers who were departing later that evening. And secondly, the Srebrenica war committee offered to General Morillon to be able to speak with journalists in Sarajevo over the communications equipment, which was in one of the rooms on the first floor of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I'm going to return to this topic shortly, but I need to diverge just very briefly. You just mentioned that videotapes were taken out of the enclave by UN military observers. Was it -- would it have been possible for officials - for example, those in the military; for example, those in the War Presidency; for example, those in whatever police forces existed - to send out material, documents -- within reason, of course, I'm not talking about bulky stuff -- but to send out material with those UNMOs who were leaving the area and with your vehicles and with your party? In other words to get stuff -- documentation out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that question as being speculative. So far this witness has given evidence of journalists, internationals giving things to UNMOs. As to whether or not anyone else could have done that, that is purely speculative, in my submission. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the witness has testified that UNMOs were able to take videotapes out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. MR. DI FAZIO: My question is, well, okay, if they're able to take videotapes out, could officials within the enclave have given them other things, like for example papers, or reports of some sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why it's speculative. Could they? I mean anything is possible. Could they have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. MR. DI FAZIO: My question is the means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, fair enough, Your Honours, if you wish to allow the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is a perfectly legitimate question and I'm sure the colonel knows exactly whether he is in a position to answer that without speculating. We don't want any speculation on your part. No guessing. You've heard the discussion, so what's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would have been able to do so. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing that it did not materially affect military operations. We would refuse absolutely to be party to anything which was assisting the military operations on one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I may return to the issue of the necessity to provide the text of the speech to the outside world, so to speak. You said the War Presidency was agreeable to this notion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency made the suggestion to General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was their idea?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was their idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was General Morillon happy with the notion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any -- what means were adopted to get the message to the outside world, the text of the speech?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found that a room next to the room where we had been meeting with the War Presidency on the first floor of the PTT building was, in fact, a fully equipped radio room with sophisticated high frequency and other radio communications equipments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber the basis for which you say that. Firstly, did you ever go in there or was it -- was this explained to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went into that room, together with General Morillon, after the General had made his speech from the -- the one that we saw on the videotapes just a moment ago. And we were taken in there by the -- by members of the War Presidency. There were radio operators in that room, and we waited five, ten minutes whilst the radio operators established communications, I believe with Sarajevo, and for the journalists at the other end to get to the radios. And then Morillon sat down, put on the headphones which were given to him by the operators, and then carried on a series of interviews with a number of journalists who, I believe, were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why do you believe that they were in Sarajevo? What makes you say that? What's the basis for your belief?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that's what the journalists said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that take, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went on and off for most of the rest of that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So -- well, more than a matter of a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was about 20 minutes and then that journalist would go. And then half an hour later, somebody from the War Presidency would come to General Morillon and say we've got another journalist, can you come and speak with him and he would go up and speak. I only went in the first couple of times because by that stage it was the same thing that was being repeated again and again. So I didn't go in for the subsequent conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there, as far as you're aware, were there any difficulties being experienced in transmitting the radio message to what you believed was Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any difficulties that the operators faced in getting that radio, that machinery to function? Not necessarily on this occasion, but on any occasion throughout the period of time you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were times that the water powered generator, which they used to create electricity, broke down a couple of times and needed fixing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain to the Trial Chamber, if you would, the - briefly - the means of generating electricity that you thought was supplying at least the radio that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the back of the PTT building there was a mountain stream of quite fast flowing water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He explained this yesterday. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did. He explained it yesterday and that was -- connected to a Dynamo, and we even heard that it supplied a little bit of electricity that was needed in the hospital too. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful, Your Honours. That's a lapse of memory on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of age, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I forgot that I'd dealt with it. Thank you, I'm grateful to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from this communication to the journalists on the day of the speech, was General Morillon or indeed yourself able to use those radio facilities at any other stage during your stay?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon used them at least once to carry on conversation with Dr. Ganic who was in the Presidency in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on the type of radio that you saw in that room and its relative sophistication or lack of sophistication.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a radio expert, but I've seen many radios and used many radios and it was a big solid commercial -- by "large" what I mean is about -- it was in a whole wall which was about two, three metres long by about three metres high and there was a bench in front, a desk and there were two operators sat in front of it. They had headphones. There were many switches, many dials. This was not something that you would go out as an individual and by in a shop. This was -- I mean, what you would expect in a PTT building. It was a big serious piece of machinery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Why didn't you use radio sets that you had, that your BH command party had, the sets, the radio sets in the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio sets that we had in our vehicles, we had two types. We had an HF radio, which is a long distance radio, which is in the UNHCR vehicle, but it was of a particular type that could only communicate with other similar radio sets that UNHCR had. And UNHCR's other radio station was in Kiseljak, in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Following that, all the activity surrounding the use of the radio set and any interviews with journalists on that day, did you and General Morillon basically retire and do nothing further on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a lot of activity because General Morillon was now welcomed as a hero and the women of the women's committee established General Morillon in two rooms on the first floor of the PTT building. They moved out mines and explosives and broken equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the -- was that on the 13th, was it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes and were those rooms made available for your party?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a small heater brought in?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that basically where you quartered yourselves for the remainder of your stay in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were tension levels diffused following the decision of General Morillon to remain in Srebrenica in the -- in the issuing of his speech?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tension was dramatically reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with the War Presidency on the following day, the 14th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what the -- what basically the topics of conversation were?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topics of conversation on that day centered mainly around what the needs of the refugees were and the desirability of getting humanitarian aid convoy in and the desirability of getting a cease-fire and cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any visit to the lines of confrontation on that day, the 14th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, in the afternoon, after meeting with the War Presidency, General Morillon persuaded them that it would be helpful for him, General Morillon, to go to the front line to meet with the Serbs in order to try and negotiate a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accompany him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else went with you to the front lines, to the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihailov went with us, obviously a Canadian crew of the armoured personnel carrier, and a Bosniak officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the Bosniak officer there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My own view is that he was there to check that we were going to do what we had promised we were going to do, but that wasn't -- that was not said out loud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or General Morillon request his presence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The War Presidency requested that he came with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio -- [Microphone not activated]. Mr. Di Fazio. Colonel, I notice in your entry on the 14th of March "Our HF comms are being jammed." Please -- MR. DI FAZIO: What page is that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 3450. Do you recall making this entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And were they being jammed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the Serbs. I see. So that was one other reason why you asked to be able to make use of the radio transmitter that was in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the day that General Morillon made the announcement, we had not yet suffered jamming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So it started precisely after that -- General Morillon had made his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Bosniak officer was there at the request of the War Presidency. You were going to speak to the Serbs at the confrontation line. Was he going to be, in your view, of any use to you in that situation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, he was a major constraint because it meant that we could not go up to, or run the risk of getting close to any Serbs because we could not run the risk of him being seen by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in those circumstances, is there any reason why you didn't take him, or rather, refused to take him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was General Morillon's decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The radio room that you have described, was it guarded?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- until the war committee suggested to General Morillon that he speak to journalists from that room, we were not even aware that it was a radio room. It was just a room which we had not been allowed into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was guarding it, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can just return to the 14th. You said that you were -- you went up to the lines of confrontation. You've told us who went, including the Bosniak officer. What topics were raised with the Serbs, if you indeed managed to speak to them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were not expecting us and we only spoke with the -- that Serb colonel who was commanding the soldiers at the section of the front line by the yellow bridge, which is on the road between Potocari and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in subsequent days, have a number of negotiations with the Serbs at this point you have called the yellow bridge?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a number of meetings, the most significant of which was with General Milovanovic who was the chief of staff of the Bosnian Serb army and who was based at Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I would just like to very briefly show you a map and ask you to indicate on it, if you can, the -- where the yellow bridge is. Thanks. Perhaps if you could put it on the ELMO, or if the usher could put it on the ELMO for you, and then if you could just mark it perhaps with a marking pen the position of the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have circled where the yellow bridge is. It was a stream which was running underneath the road. And the Serb front lines were immediately on that side of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please put an initial next to the part that you have marked on the plan, on the map, and then sign the map wherever you like and then we'll give it a number. I thank you kindly. So this will be P515; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, 515. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've dealt with the map and finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now want you to just look at an entry in your diary, please. The portion of your diary that I am interested in you will find in the photocopied section at 3463 to 3464 and 3465. I apologise for skipping around a bit, but it's -- firstly, if you go to 3463, our photocopy is not very clear. Can you see the date that's actually -- that those entries relate to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me refer to my diary, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my diary, it says 15 March 1200 TACSAT message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could we have the page put on the ELMO please, for the public to be able to follow. Thank you. Sorry for having interrupted you in the way I did. I apologise to you. Yes, you were saying in my diary it says 15 March, 1200.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: TACSAT message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those messages relating to events that had happened on the previous day, the 14th?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either the previous day or earlier that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It contemplates, if you look at 3463, halfway down the page, referring to what General Morillon is going to do "a request of the UN Security Council to disclose ..." Sorry. What's that word, D -- declare, "... declare the region of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, Cerska, Skelani a UN-protected area. He will propose this to General Mladic at a meeting between Bratunac and Srebrenica at 1500 hours today." Now, had that notion or idea been raised the day before, that is the 14th?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the meeting that was to take place on the 15th of March at 3.00 in the afternoon, between Bratunac and Srebrenica, was that also the yellow bridge?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The second message that you appear to have wanted to send out was to a General Jones for onward transmission to the BH command in Kiseljak. Namely that Srebrenica was subject to continuous shelling and bombing at a low rate until arrival. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until the arrival of General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say not a shell has fallen in the town since General Morillon's arrival.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a reflection of reality as far as you're --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn the page over. There are a number of topics that we may as well deal with here. Page 3464. It's item number 3 that I am interested in. You say, "There are 3 groupings in the ..." -- well, I can't understand?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the area".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- "in the area: Local population, refugees and soldiers. Little coordination between the three groups." What precisely did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that the local population appeared to be doing very little for the refugees and that the soldiers were not doing anything for the local population and the soldiers were doing their own activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then there is an entry -- in fact, could you read it out please starting with the word "there is"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There is, in addition, a radical clan who are manipulating these groups and issue propaganda and control the 'amateur radio'".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think if you continue reading, you have to -- in effect, if you look over to page 365 in order to understand it, I think it is the sentence is "It is they?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is they who --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- who encourage the refugees to block General Morillon."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. So who is the radical clan that you had in mind there? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not know for sure, but the War Presidency certainly had something to do with it and soldiers certainly had something else to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference there to amateur radio. What amateur radio is that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that stage in the conflict, there had been numerous reports in international press quoting amateur radio reports from Srebrenica and Gorazde. Having seen the level of sophistication of the radio equipment that they did have, we were -- we did not believe the representation of such radio operators as "amateur".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "having seen the level the level of sophistication of the radio equipment that they did have," are you referring to what you've told us about the sets that you saw in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And a second set that I happened to have seen in the Presidency building in Sarajevo earlier, before we went into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm talking about Srebrenica, though. Thank you. Thank you. I've finished with that entry. If we can now just jump back to the 14th. You had a meeting at the yellow bridge. Just, again, tell us what the general result of that meeting was, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting had been requested with General Mladic, however General Mladic did not turn up. It was General Milovanovic, his chief of staff, who actually turned up instead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he able to assist you much in negotiating in any significant way?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. He took away messages and undertook to get back to General Morillon through Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarize, for the Trial Chamber, the most important matters that you raised with General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first issue we wanted to discuss was cessation of hostilities by the Serbs. The second issue was cease-fires. Third issue was the deployment of UN military observers in order to monitor the cease-fire. We also asked about -- we also discussed evacuation of injured -- of injured people and the establishment of helicopter corridors in order to be able to evacuate injured. Milovanovic said that no -- we also wanted the humanitarian convoys which were blocked at Zvornik to be allowed free passage through to Srebrenica. Milovanovic said that until General Morillon left Srebrenica, no humanitarian convoys would be allowed through. Regarding the deployment of UN military observers, I think he said he had no authority about it and he would get back to us about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the ostensible concern of the Serbs was concerning General Morillon? Why were they worried about his leaving Srebrenica? Did they provide you with an explanation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just said that -- they insisted for General Morillon's safety that he leave the -- leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that was not a concern of General Morillon? Or am I incorrect?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event, you made arrangements to meet again at the yellow bridge the next day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but that was in order to receive the -- the humanitarian aid convoy, it was not in order to meet with Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you eventually -- did an aid convoy eventually come into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A convoy eventually came in a number of days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number of days later, okay. Let's just keep with those dates. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, in summary, what you did on the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that we went back to the yellow bridge in order to try and meet the convoy, which never turned up. And we had further meetings with members of the War Presidency and with our UNMOs, our UN military observers, who had been into the Srebrenica enclave who had reports about what military activities had been going on. And I spent a lot of time preparing reports and reporting back to Kiseljak over the UNHCR radio and over the tactical satellite radio, to Frankfurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Can I ask you now to turn your attention to the following day again, the 17th of March. We're moving along. On that particular day, can you recall the basic outline of events up until the evening? And I'll get to the evening in more detail later. But firstly, the day's events: Did you go up to the yellow bridge again?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went up to the yellow bridge every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall who you met on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the local Serb commander, the same colonel who we'd met on the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for going up there on that particular day? Was it again connected with the possible arrival of the aid convoy, or the other reasons that you've mentioned; cease-fires, demilitarisation and so on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to primarily get the convoy through. There wasn't much sense talking with the local colonel about cease-fires and demilitarisation because he simply didn't have the authority to...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to turn your attention to the evening. Did you speak to anyone not in your party that night?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke with the War Presidency earlier in the evening. And later in the evening, Colonel Oric turned up in the PTT building in Srebrenica and had a long conversation with General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Oric -- let me rephrase that. Did you expect Colonel Oric to turn up? Was it by appointment, in other words?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. We had been asking the war committee to pass on messages to Colonel Oric saying we wanted to meet with him, every day. And suddenly he turned up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had been the reaction of the War Presidency when you passed those messages to them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked them, please, we need to speak with Colonel Oric, and they said that they had no control over him and they promised to pass on General Morillon's requests to him, but could not promise anything about when he would turn up, or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall about what time he turned up?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about -- about 7.00 in the evening. It was well after dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dressed in similar way he had been dressed when we'd met him in Konjevic Polje; in dark green thick, heavy - what I call winter uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he turn up alone or in company with others?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he may or may not have turned up with because I only saw him in the PTT building itself. And there were many Bosniak soldiers who -- I mean, I didn't know where they came from, or who they were or who they were with, because he was suddenly there and went into this room that I described earlier that had been allocated to General Morillon on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The room that the women's committee had cleaned up for you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now ask you about some entries relating to the 17th and we may touch upon this topic, but firstly I would like to be clear as to where your entries for the 17th actually start. Can I ask you to look at 3497 -- I'm sorry. 3495. Is that where your entries for the 17th of March start?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I must look in my --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Sure, if you wouldn't mind doing that.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My entries for the 17th of March start earlier. They start on the page with your reference number 3491.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you. And do the entries for the 17th continue all the way to 3502?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, though there will be entries after that which refer back to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to, yes. I've got that. Thanks. In fact, if you turn the page back to 3501, I think we can actually see a fairly clear date there. 1800, 17th of March. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is up here. I'm pointing it out now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can start with the text that I'm interested in. Go to 3502. Our photocopy is not terribly clear in the middle of the page. Could you just read out the heading of that entry at 3502.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Meeting in Srebrenica PTT building, Morillon, Naser Oric, 19.15."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a reference to the meeting that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was at this meeting? Were you present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mihailov?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihailov, and Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And there entries appear. Can you just read out the first entry. I think it is, "Oric reported..."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Oric reported strong attacks from north-west and south-east. Tregovac has fallen."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I just want to ask you. What precisely did he report to you about that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Colonel Oric was describing to General Morillon was the military situation in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to be sure that we're clear about this. He was describing events in the north-west of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And events in the south-east of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what he actually said about the military events in those two reaches of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall specifically what he said, but what I can recall is the overall context, which was that the military situation was very dire and was very bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a military man; was it a clear, coherent military description of events?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly. It was as clear as was possible with somebody with the difficulties he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no ability to move. He did not have reliable communications. It was the best that could be expected from somebody in his situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's what -- thank you. Thank you. He was obviously labouring under many handicaps that many other military commanders might not have had. But was that your impression?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go on to the next entry. Can you please read out the text of that so that it's clear because it's not --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Many tanks gathering on western side of north-west corner. Expect big push tomorrow. Expect attack tomorrow along the route we came in along." This was referring to the route over the mountains which General Morillon and I had used to enter into the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Pause there. Was it Mr. Oric, Colonel Oric who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue reading out the next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Have discussed proposal of demilitarising area. Want to place whole zone immediately under UNPROFOR control (Cerska - Srebrenica). Need to deploy observers along Drina and check crossings. Dr. Ganic accepts".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you discuss the -- proposition, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Proposal for the demilitarisation with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had -- rather, General Morillon had initially discussed this with Dr. Ganic, using the war committee's radio. He had secondly discussed it with the Srebrenica War Presidency. And he was now discussing it with Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had been the attitude of Dr. Ganic and what had been the attitude of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Ganic had broadly accepted the proposal and wanted it to happen. The War Presidency had broadly accepted the proposal, with some caveats that they had said they did not want any Serbs to enter the town and only police men would be allowed in and they wanted the UN to guarantee this. Colonel Oric refused and said that he would never surrender or never give up his arms, he would now allow demilitarisation and that he would fight inside Srebrenica -- in amongst the houses to the end, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the consequences for you, for you and your party, for General Morillon, given the situation that had developed with the approval of Ganic, the qualified approval of the War Presidency and now this refusal?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon was very concerned, because this is a bigger issue. One of the reasons that the Serbs had given for continuing their attacks and not ceasing hostilities was the ongoing attacks outside of the Srebrenica enclave by Bosniak forces. What General Morillon was seeking to -- was trying to achieve was agreement to the cessation of hostilities out of the enclave by the Bosniaks in order to remove the excuse from the Serbs from continuing their operations. So what General Morillon was trying to achieve was to get Colonel Oric to agree not to continue with attacks out of the enclave. That was the first point. The second point is that, General Morillon was very anxious that -- or very concerned that Colonel Oric would continue fighting even if it was in amongst the town because that would cause many casualties. And I think he used the words "one shell landing anywhere will injure tons of people".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the topic of the cessation or possible cessation of attacks from out of the enclave discussed during this encounter?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In some detail. General Morillon asked Colonel Oric to stop his attacks and Colonel Oric said that he could not stop his attacks because he relied upon attacks that he made in order to capture weapons, ammunition, food and supplies and he said to General Morillon, "Where do you think my bullets come from? Every bullet that we use to defend ourselves is taken from the Serbs".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Morillon counter his arguments in any way or offer any reasons as to allay his fears or concerns?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said to Colonel Oric that the Serbs had complained about massacres of civilians and were using these accusations as their excuse for continuing their attacks against the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall a response, if any, of Colonel Oric to this reasoning?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Oric's response was that, yes, sadly, sometimes his men did go beyond what was necessary and sometimes they killed ten people, when in fact it would only be necessary to kill five to secure the supplies that they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where matters rested or was there more discussion about this very topic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The topic moved on to prisoners, because the Serbs had claimed that the Bosniaks were holding Serb prisoners in Srebrenica. And General Morillon said, "Surely it's pointless holding prisoners, as you'd only have to feed them". And Colonel Oric's response was "Yes. Taking prisoners is not really practical and we don't do it". He went on to -- but he never responded -- General Morillon asked him a couple of times, "Are you holding any prisoners?" And he didn't respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the Serb -- you said the Serbs had made the claim that the Bosniaks were holding Serb prisoners in Srebrenica. Do you know who, which particular Serb made that allegation or claim?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Colonel at the front line at the yellow bridge at Bratunac. The Serb Colonel in command in Bratunac itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the demeanour of Colonel Oric during this meeting that you've just been describing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very depressed. He was very anxious. He was totally different to when we had seen him in cost of Konjevic Polje. In Konjevic Polje he had been a confident, in difficult circumstances, man. Calm. Measured. Balanced. Whereas the Oric who we saw that evening was very depressed, very low, and almost confiding in General Morillon about his difficulties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that had elapsed between I think the 5th -- the 6th of March when you spoke to him and this encounter on the 17th about eleven days or so, had the Serbs continued when pressed on with their attacks around the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is continually, yes, and that by that stage, the road from Zvornik to Pale which we looked at on the map yesterday had been freed and was clear and the Bosniaks had been pushed all the way back from there. We also understood that they had suffered -- they had lost many villages down in the south-east of the enclave as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just go back to the entries, please. The next entry, please, on 3503. Could you just read that out. I think it's -- start at the top, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very top it says: "Later need to consider all of eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's referring to the previous one, where we spoke about demilitarisation. Then it leads on, "M" for General Morillon, "peace still possible provided Serbs not crazy enough to attack Srebrenica. Serbs still claiming they attack because Halilovic attacking Tuzla, Ilijas. As long as no order countermanding these attacks, they will continue." Then "O" for Oric, "order given two days ago to cease offensive. Most important to cease offensive and ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to, please go back to entry "M" which you say refers to General Morillon. Can you explain more carefully what General Morillon was driving at when he made those comments.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon was being very careful not to make accusations to Colonel Oric and was using the accusations and behaviors of the Serbs as the reason for please stopping your activities, your offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you understand reference to be to the attacks of Halilovic to be?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Halilovic had at the beginning of March on Sarajevo radio, made a pronouncement in which he had ordered all Bosniak soldiers to attack towards Srebrenica and Gorazde, with all vigor. This was broadcast over public radio and obviously was heard by the Serbs. And the Serbs used this as a reason for continuing their offensives and said they would not stop their offensives until Halilovic withdrew that order, because as far as they were concerned, as long as that order was not publicly withdrawn over the radio, then they were breaking any attempt to make a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall if Colonel Oric was -- appeared to be aware of this order and this offensive that you've just spoken of?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then turn to the entry -- under "O" for Oric. "Order given two days ago to cease offensive. Most important to cease offensive." What do you recall Colonel Oric saying about that, in other words, can you flesh out that entry, please and tell us -- provide us more details.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that he told General Morillon that he had received the order two days ago, in other words, from Sarajevo, to cease his offensive actions. But it was very important for the Serbs to cease their offensive as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would that be an appropriate moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Di Fazio. Stop here. Have a break. 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. I need your indulgence for a minute or so. We have succeeded in moving tomorrow's and Thursday's sittings from the afternoon to the morning, if, that is, of course, agreeable to Defence and Prosecution. Prosecution, I suppose it doesn't make any difference to you because you will be here in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we will immediately update the issues as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously it depends to a certain extent on the schedule. I assume I would probably be starting cross-examining tomorrow. I can probably fill the day with my cross-examination tomorrow, if pushed. Obviously it slightly reduces the time for preparing, but I think I will be in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are at that, are you finishing today with your in-chief? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I hope to finish today. If I don't finish today, I will be almost to the very end of my examination-in-chief. There's a good chance I'll finish today. But I -- I can reassure the chamber that if I don't it's not going to take up much of tomorrow at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Jones, how much time do you require for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will be about two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we better not take risks. Basically we'll have -- yes. And then for Friday, do you have any other witness prepared for Friday in case we have time to start with a new witness or not, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have scheduled on the 17th when it is on the 18th. That's fine with us to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Okay. So you should be okay. There shouldn't be any problems. You will have as much time as you require, obviously. So tomorrow, Wednesday 16th March, we will be sitting in this courtroom at 9.00, starting at 9.00. And Thursday, we will sit in courtroom 3, also at 9.00. Then I will have an initial appearance which now I need to move from 5:30 to 2.30 on Thursday, but the good news is that the initial appearance will not eat up from our time in Oric. All right. I thank you for your cooperation. Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before the break we were talking about this encounter that you had with Colonel Oric on the 17th and the notes that you made in your diary. Could you please look in your diary to the page that bears ERN number 3504. In fact it is the next page, basically, from the point that we were looking at. Now, firstly, the date. Again on our photocopy it is not entirely clear. It appears to be the 18th of March. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it reads 0800, 18 March. 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the entries from the 18th of March start from this point?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn over the page, please, to 3505. And the entries there are, with all due respect, a lot clearer. "Sitrep in Dutch." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that I was speaking over the UNHCR HF radio with a Dutch officer in Kiseljak and that I made my report in Dutch, in order to make it more difficult for the Serbs to understand what it was we were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it may well be known, I don't know, but sitrep is, I think, a situation report?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read the first entry.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first entry is "Naser Oric returned to Srebrenica for first time, a long discussion with commander." By "commander" I mean General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that a reference to a discussion you had the previous evening?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the next entry.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "2. Military situation now deteriorating rapidly, losing five villages a day. At current rate we'll have nothing left in two weeks."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who provided you with that military assessment? Was that your own or did you get it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That came from Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next entry. Read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Heavy offensive to north-west and south-east."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, the source of information for that entry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next entry, read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At number 4, "locals reported four aircraft attacking villages around Osmace again yesterday. Cannot confirm this." By "locals" what I meant was local military in Srebrenica, as opposed to Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next entry, number five.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five. "Oric talked about fighting to the last man in the town, if necessary."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you've already given evidence that that came up in the previous evening?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 6.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This would be a catastrophe as town is already so crowded that any shell would injure tens of people."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose assessment was that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was General Morillon's assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn over the page to 3506. I certainly don't want to take you through that chapter and verse, but what basically does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to other conversations and communications that we had had, that we were trying to get the convoy with humanitarian aid which was stuck in Zvornik into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that also to be a part of the content of a radio message?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please turn over the page to 3507. I think at the top there is a handwritten -- it's all handwritten. But at the top there is a notation dealing with some events that had allowed you to have more rations and food to keep your party going for a longer time in Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The main part that I am interested in commences after that. "Situation report for General Jones to pass on to BH command." Who is General Jones?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Jones was a brigadier general in the United States marine corps who was an advisor to the US commander of NATO forces based in Frankfurt. And General Jones was the person who had supplied major -- a US intelligence major and a tactical satellite radio to come with General Morillon when he went into Srebrenica in order to liaise regarding the air drops of humanitarian aid which were happening most nights in the Srebrenica enclave. This radio was in a rucksack and was secure; in other words, it was encrypted. In other words, the Serbs could not understand what it was we were saying. The only disadvantage was that the stations at the other end of that net were in Frankfurt. So they then had to pass anything from Frankfurt to Kiseljak, but it was our only means of secure communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next entry military situation, can you just read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One military situation, A, Naser Oric commander of Srebrenica enclave arrived in Srebrenica last night for first meeting with General Morillon."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think I need to take you through all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. With regard to this particular entry: I see that this entry seems to me as if it has been crossed out or cancelled. What are those three oblique lines across it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are they of your own making? Or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I -- if you look through my notes, sir, you will find many crossings out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did, actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I did was, as I completed a section, I then crossed it out so that it was clear in my mind that I finished that particular report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's a fair enough explanation. At least we have an explanation. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to take you through this in minute detail. If you look at the remaining entries, you can see that the -- there is a commentary on the situation, the deteriorating military situation, the commentary on the loss of villages and the rate of loss of villages. Commentary on the attacks from the north-west and south-east. Is that a reference to the content of discussions that you had the previous evening with Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was principally based on what Colonel Oric told us. It was also based on information from the -- our own UN military observers who had been out in the area and made observations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And again there is, the last main entry, "local commanders repeated that the villages in the Osmace area were bombed by aircraft." And I think you've already given a description of where you got that evidence from.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The entry keeps going. If you look at it, number 1, at 3507, is the military situation. Do you see that? We've just been through it. Do you see military situation, number 1?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. At the bottom of the page, number 2, refugee situation. Then you provide entries at 3508, concerning refugee issues. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those matters relating to refugees also part of the situation report to General Jones?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Go to number 3, and you see that there is, again, a reference to "Meeting with Naser Oric last night." In fact, could you please read out the remainder of that entry to the bottom of page 3508 so we can always be sure of the actual words.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Meeting with Naser Oric last night. Oric is Bosnian commander Srebrenica pocket. General Morillon last met him at Konjevic Polje on 6th March, 1993. "a. Bosnian military authorities are desperate that morale is rock bottom. "b. Oric stated he and his soldiers would fight to bitter end in Srebrenica if necessary. General Morillon trying to persuade him this would be folly. Srebrenica is so crowded that every shell hitting the town would injure dozens. "c. General Morillon discussed conditions for making Srebrenica an open town under UN protection."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those matters are all fairly self-explanatory, but entry C interests me: "General Morillon discussed conditions for making Srebrenica an open town under UN protection." With whom did General Morillon discuss that topic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He discussed it with Colonel Oric and with the Srebrenica war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this also part of the text -- rather, the content of the radio message to General Jones?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Turn the page over to 3509. Item number 4. I won't ask you to read that out as the writing is relatively clear there. It's obviously a reference to "a meeting with the president of the war committee 9.30 this morning."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have in fact a meeting with the president of the war committee at 9.30 on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And the notations there are that they speak for themselves, the president said that he'd be -- the Bosnians are willing to hand over their weapons on certain conditions; the cessation of the Serb offensive, UNPROFOR guarantee of no military, no Serb military and police, and the fact of approval by Dr. Ganic. And the request to Security Council for a declaration of protected status. Were those topics, in fact, discussed with the War Presidency, with the president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Item number five, commander's assessment. Is that General Morillon's assessment?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I would ask you to read that out to the end of the message which you can see over the following page at 3510. So if you can read the commander's assessment entirely.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "5. Commander's assessment. General Morillon considers that opening of an air corridor for helicopters remains one of the major conditions to guarantee the safety of the population and to guarantee the safety of the evacuation of the wounded men. General Morillon --" it then turns over the page -- "requests BH command, UNPROFOR's, Zagreb and EUCOM --" EUCOM is the Frankfurt US command -- "to exercise all their influence to achieve this objective." End of message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- looking at the entry at 3509, it's clear that the president of the committee, the War Presidency in Srebrenica, according to this message anyway, is agreeable to a demilitarisation of sorts, the handing over of weapons, which I take to mean demilitarisation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were -- let me -- let me withdraw that question. Did you give any thought or consideration as to how you could possibly achieve this if Colonel Oric had indicated his intention that there would be fighting until the end?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon was very concerned about that and when he had spoken with Colonel Oric the previous evening, Colonel Oric had said that he didn't -- he didn't care what the war committee said, he was going to fight to the end and he was never going to hand any of his weapons over, and he was very dismissive of the war committee and he did not think very much of them. General Morillon tried to -- and continually tried to persuade Colonel Oric to stop his attacks in order to remove the excuse from the Serbs for continuing their offensives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Can I ask you, if you can, to amplify part of your answer. You say that General Morillon continually tried to persuade him to stop his attacks. When did that continually happen, because you've only described an encounter in the early part of March around the 5th or 6th, on both days with Colonel Oric, and again the previous evening that you're talking about, the 17th of March. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what you mean by "continually trying to persuade him."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Continually" means on the previous evening throughout that meeting. It means also at a brief meeting that we had later, around the 21st of March, and again at a meeting that General Morillon had with Colonel Oric on about the 23rd of March. On each of those occasions it was a constant refrain of General Morillon's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any alteration in the attitude of Colonel Oric at all on any of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main conversation was the one on the previous evening when he said that he had to continue attacking in order to acquire the means with which to defend the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Can I ask you to describe the events of the 18th of March 1993. Obviously this radio message was sent at some point. How did the rest of the day pan out?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the rest of the day was, again, a journey down to the yellow bridge to try and meet with the humanitarian aid convoy and other communications and coordinations with Kiseljak in order to progress the work that Morillon was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have meetings with the War Presidency? Or members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this meeting with the president of the war committee that we've just -- we've just been through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see Colonel Oric that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Oric had left the previous evening in the same way that he had come. He just was suddenly there and he was suddenly gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have meetings with the Serbs at the line of confrontation on that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.
