utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th and the 20th of March, did you see Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the line of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On both days?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On both days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the yellow bridge?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whom did you meet on those days?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th we met with the same Serb colonel. On the 20th, we again met with the same Serb colonel, however, on the way down to the yellow bridge -- this was the first day that we had taken not only the armoured personnel carrier but also a Jeep with us. And I was in the armoured personnel carrier and was playing with the radio in the armoured personnel carrier and suddenly managed to pick up the UN aid convoy which was stuck in Zvornik and actually had live communications with them and established where they were. I told General Morillon this, and when we got to the Serb front line, General Morillon told me, "You stay here with the armoured personnel carrier and keep the front line open, because the excuse that was usually used to prevent humanitarian aid convoys passing was that there's fighting going on, so Pyers, you stay here. I will take the Jeep and go to Zvornik and try and get the convoy unblocked."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Just -- I think there is a little mistake in the transcript. You're talking now about the 19th of March, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you? Thank you for clarifying that. The 20th. Thank you. Was there any success with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About six hours later. We had gone down to the front line at about 10.00, 10.30. About six hours later, at 4.00 in the afternoon, General Morillon turned up at the head of the convoy and we then took the convoy, we then led the convoy over the front line and the confrontation line and into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trucks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ten trucks, ten-ton trucks from the Dutch Belgian transport battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were they carrying?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were carrying foodstuffs in almost all of the trucks. There were one or two trucks which had sugar and medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you take the trucks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We initially stopped the trucks outside the PTT building in order to find out from the war committee where they wanted the trucks unloaded. Members of the war committee then guided the convoy further into Srebrenica, into the centre of Srebrenica, to a place where they wanted the foodstuffs to be unloaded out of the trucks into the cellar of a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that process went ahead reasonably smoothly in all the circumstances, or not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It went -- it took most of the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. When you say that on this occasion you met with members of the war committee, did you meet with the entire number of members and would you recollect who you met with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one person I always remember was Hajrudin Avdic, the president, and unless he was there we didn't have any meaningful conversations. And it was him who told us to follow the guide and we then followed the guide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And were the medicines kept with the sugar and taken to the same storage place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The medicines were unloaded straight into the hospital, which was opposite the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On whose instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The instructions of somebody from the war committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you met Dr. Mukanovic on this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was around. I cannot confirm whether or not he is the one who said where to unload or not. He was certainly around, though the instructions were given to the officers of the convoy and I wasn't actually present when the instructions were given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you given any thought to where you were going to deposit all of the materials that you brought in, apart from the medicines? The food, I mean.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were concerned, because we knew, as a rule, that by our own estimation, only about 20 percent of the humanitarian aid delivered in Bosnia ever reached the refugees who needed it, because invariably we were required, as part of the agreement by which the UN was in Bosnia, to deliver humanitarian aid to the local authorities. And we were concerned that if we gave the aid to the local authorities, that they would use most of it for their own purposes and would not give it to the refugees. So we were skeptical, but we had no choice but to hand over the supplies to the local authorities, which, in this case, was the Srebrenica war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I'm interested in. There was no question about it, you were obliged to ascertain who the local authorities were and deliver the aid to those persons?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, and it was something that caused us a lot of frustration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only people you spoke to, or as far as you're aware your party spoke to, were the members of the Srebrenica War Presidency concerning the location of the food?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And whilst the food was being unloaded, the War Presidency -- Hajrudin Avdic and a number of their members, and I and Mihailov and Mukanovic all walked up from the PTT building to where the food was being unloaded and stood there for some time, watching the food being unloaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You specifically recall Dr. Mukanovic being present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just take the witness back to page 3508 and it's paragraph C. This is part of the report sent or meant to be sent to General Jones to pass on to the command in Frankfurt, as I understood you before. In paragraph C there is, "Have seen some evidence of food distribution; some --" I can't read that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Some more of the antibiotics."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "... dropped two days ago has been handed in to the hospital." I ask you to amplify a little bit on this and also tell me whether this could have had an effect on your and General Morillon's, on the 20th, you had this convoy finally succeed to pass through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This paragraph C is referring to food which was dropped by aircraft every night. And it was a -- it was a vicious, it was a horrible situation because the air drops were carried out at night and the air drops were in pallets of about between 400 and 700 kilograms, which were not dropped with parachutes but which were dropped with drogue parachutes which simply slow down and keep the pallet the right way up. The pallet had about a metre of cardboard in that to take the impact when it landed, but these things were dropped at night and the noise of these things coming down with the drogue parachute was like an express train. You couldn't see where they would land and if they landed on top of you, you were dead. Every night we were told that between ten and fifteen people were killed because people would go out at night to open areas where the air drops were landing and people -- it was the law of the jungle. It was the law of the fittest, because the first person to reach a pallet, that would be then his pallet and he would hold on to that, and there were reports of knife fights and the doctors in the hospital reported that they were having to treat people for knife injuries because the refugees were fighting for the aid. We requested the air drops to be moved further away from Srebrenica so that the food would be dropped and it could be collected and could then be distributed in a more organised manner, rather than this bitter fight for survival, which was what had been happening in the nights up until then. We had also in a previous communication requested antibiotics because it was the top priority of the doctors in the hospital. And we had been told in advance over the TACSAT radio that one aircraft would have antibiotics and it would drop slightly off to the side, and, however, refugees got to the -- got to the package first and most of the antibiotics just disappeared. But we told the Srebrenica war committee and said, Look antibiotics were dropped last night, can you please tell your people they can't use them, please hand in any antibiotics that they've picked up or found into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Our client is suddenly feeling rather unwell. I wonder if it would be possible to have a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Mr. Jones. Certainly, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can take instructions as to how long perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we will do is we will have a break now for as long as necessary. And you will communicate with the registrar what the position -- what the situation is and what are the requirements of your client and we will take the necessary decisions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it needs to be to stop sitting completely, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indications are it should be -- thank you. Indications are it shouldn't be too long. I think it's a question of faintness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever time he requires. We will have a short break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our client is feeling better now and I think we are now prepared to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, but I do want to make it clear, on behalf of the Bench, that our interpretation or our understanding of the right of the accused to be present throughout the whole, the entire proceedings necessarily entails also his being able to follow what is taking place, what is happening. So if, at any time, in spite of his presence here, he is not in a condition to follow, he is feeling either -- anyway, he knows best. If there are problems, do bring that to our attention straight away and we will decide what to do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're welcome. Mr. Di Fazio. Yes, one moment because we stopped at a time when I had something on my mind, and I need to go back to the page. Yes. Colonel, you were explaining to the Chamber, to the Trial Chamber, what lay behind your entry, paragraph C, that I drew your attention to earlier on. And particularly you had arrived at the point where, with regard to antibiotics that were included in the pallets that were being dropped from the air. You were being told -- you were telling the war committee, informing the war committee members about them and that to have them recovered, if possible, and have them handed over to the hospital. En passant, you did mention that you had been told on several occasions by the doctors of the great need that there was for these antibiotics in the hospital. When you say you were being told by the doctors, were you including Dr. Mukanovic amongst them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was referring to the doctor in the hospital and the Medecins Sans Frontieres doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss these air drops from antibiotics with Dr. Mukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no reason to discuss it with him. We did say to the -- to Hajrudin Avdic that we had requested antibiotics and medicines to be dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did Dr. Mukanovic ever make any specific request to you or General Morillon or anyone else in your -- to your troop about the need for antibiotics or any other kind of medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was one of the things that puzzled us, as to what he was doing in the Presidency, what was he doing there and why. We didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told His Honour that Dr. Mukanovic never said anything to you about the need for antibiotics, and as I read it, the need for any other kind of medicines.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did he discuss any, any health issue of any description whatsoever with you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we got onto this topic of air drops and medical supplies, you were telling us about the convoy that had come in on the 20th and the unloading of it which continued into the night. Were you present throughout the night or not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was only present for 20 minutes, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spent the night in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you now to turn your attention to the following day, the 21st of March. That day, in the morning, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had made arrangements to go to Bratunac to meet with General Gvero and I was making preparations to depart from the PTT building. By "preparations," what I mean is that it took about half an hour to start the armoured personnel carrier in the cold and we needed to clear snow off the vehicles. And as I was doing this, together with the crew of the vehicle, I suddenly heard a loud car engine, automobile engine, and I looked up and saw a black Mercedes driving at high speed through the town from the direction of the centre of the town towards the PTT building. It was a Mercedes with a dark smoke-coloured windows and low profile tyres, the sort of thing that looked totally out of place in Srebrenica. And I couldn't believe my eyes. I was astonished. This car came screeching to a halt in a hand brake turn and out of the car climbed Colonel Oric and a couple of bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there. Did you happen to notice what sort of plates it was carrying?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it had German number plates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the car approached, were there people in the street?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few people in the street and the car was driven recklessly and people were diving out of the way of the car as it came roaring down the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue your narrative, please. You told us the car turns up with a hand brake turn and Colonel Oric gets out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Oric strode out of the car up to the -- towards the PTT building and wanted to speak with General Morillon. I got General Morillon. He came down. And through Mihailov, Colonel Oric said, "Follow me. Come with me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you follow him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By that stage we had just started the armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you this: Did you know where you were going?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or why you were going?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got into the armoured personnel carrier and followed the black Mercedes which went back in the direction of the centre of town and stopped halfway to the centre of town, 300 metres from the PTT building, 500 metres from the PTT building, something like that. Colonel Oric got out and walked into a house which was at the side of the -- side of the road which, coming from the direction of the PTT building, was to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Can I just ask you to pause your narrative there. You said it was a house. Now, do you mean a private residence of some sort?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I mean a private house. Not an office or a shop or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember if it was an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was definitely not an apartment building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you might call a bungalow style house, single story or --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It had two stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he came back out of the house and about two minutes, three minutes later, two Bosniak soldiers appeared with a man, supporting a man between them, and Colonel Oric said to General Morillon, "Take him back to his people." And this man had been a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And was apparently a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you, at that stage, accompanied by -- I know Morillon was with you, General Morillon was with you, but were you accompanied with other soldiers in your party?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had the armoured personnel carrier, in other words the Canadian crew of the armoured personnel carrier, and Mihailov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have head gear?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colour of the head gear, please?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing the blue UN helmets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can you describe to the Trial Chamber the condition of this individual.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man looked like the Jews who were rescued in 1945 from the German concentration camps. His arms were like sticks, his stomach was completely sunk. He was unable to stand. He appeared unable to speak. We got a stretcher out from the armoured personnel carrier. We laid him on this stretcher and he managed to move his arms up as if to protect his head. Mihailov spoke to him in Serbo-Croat and said, "It's okay, it's okay. We're going to take you to hospital," and then he relaxed a bit, but he looked -- he opened his eyes and he was very, very frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if he had his wits about him, if he was fully orientated or did he appear confused?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appeared very confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you -- what did you do with him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We turned the armoured personnel carrier around. We put him into the back of the armoured personnel carrier on the stretcher, turned the armoured personnel carrier around and drove to the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hand -- did you hand him over?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were at the yellow bridge, we stopped and called over Serbs, soldiers, and Mihailov explained we had a person who needed evacuation, and about five minutes later, an ambulance arrived from the direction of Bratunac and one of the Serb militia soldiers said that he thought he recognised the man and thought he knew who he was and that he was a local. He was put into the Serb ambulance and driven off up from the yellow bridge towards the Bratunac. That was the last I saw of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the rest of the day pan out? What did you do for the remainder of the day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We then went to the meeting that had been scheduled in Bratunac, and in fact again we had been promised that Mladic would be there, but Mladic didn't turn up again, and it was General Gvero who was there. We met with him and the mayor of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to look at your diary again, please. And can I ask you to go to page -- well, ERN number 3536, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I can see more clearly on the ELMO. There's a date there that's clear, the 21st of March, I think.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is 21st of March, 2100, by TACSAT to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, is this the content of a radio message that you sent?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first of a series of radio messages that I sent to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At about 9 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By that stage, the Americans had provided another TACSAT radio to Kiseljak, so instead of us having to speak to Frankfurt for General Jones in Frankfurt to then relay information, the Americans had now provided a TACSAT to Kiseljak so that we were able to speak directly to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the entry that I am interested is the first one there, you can see it I think under number 1 that looks vaguely like a "7," okay?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you can just read it out.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We released a wounded Serb prisoner. We know of two more Serbs held by Bosnian forces in Srebrenica who commander is trying to get released."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. First line, please, "We released a wounded Serb prisoner." What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reference to the events earlier that day that I described to you a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you -- the next two lines: "We know of two more Serbs held by Bosnian forces in Srebrenica." What are you talking about and what is your source of knowledge about two more Serbs held by Bosnian forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that Colonel Oric said that he had two more prisoners. General Morillon was pressing him, How many prisoners do you have? Don't hold on to them. Release them. That he said that he had two more, but that they were common criminals and nothing to do with fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when had that conversation taken place, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the prisoner was brought out or...

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bear in mind that it was General Morillon who told me this. I did not hear that myself. It was General Morillon who told me that he'd been told that, that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you. I will move on to another topic. Can I ask you to turn your attention to the next day, to the next day, which is the 22nd of March. You've already mentioned a place called Kravica. Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, we went to a funeral in Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the people who had been excavated from Kravica, and we were then taken, after the funeral, in a convoy by the Serbs to Kravica itself and we there saw --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will get on to that in just a moment, if I can just interrupt you. First of all, go back to the funeral in Bratunac. Were members of the Serb leadership present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Gvero and Madam Plavsic were present, together with a large number of other Serb colonels, who I didn't recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had been invited to this funeral?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Gvero had the previous day asked General Morillon to attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was your attendance at the funeral purely and simply for the funeral or did you discuss matters touching the sorts of issues that we've been talking about the last two days?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, General Gvero had the previous day apologised for General Mladic not turning up and had said that General Mladic would be at the funeral, which is one reason for General Morillon wanting to attend, to speak with Mladic, but Mladic was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you said that following the funeral, you went to Kravica. Can you describe to the Trial Chamber what you saw in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to a place where there is a road close to a stream and the stream was about 20, 30 metres away from the road, and down by the edge of the stream there were a number of holes which had been dug up. And there were about three or four people in white coveralls who looked as if they were carrying out forensic analysis of things they told us were bodies which had been dug up out of those holes. Over to the side there was a pile of partially decomposed bodies, and next to the pile of bodies there was a agricultural trailer, which had, again, about 15 or 20 partially decomposed bodies in it. We were then taken to some buildings which were the other side of the road, and there was a barn in which we were taken, and we were shown a wall inside this barn in which there were a large number of holes which we were told were bullet holes, and that the people who had been buried down by the river had all been killed up against that wall and shot and that they, the Serbs, knew this because one person had seen this and had managed to managed to escape and had reported exactly what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Following these events in Kravica and Bratunac, did you return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. Would Your Honours just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I will ask you to return to the diary again now, please. I would ask that you look at entry 3540. Now, at the top of the page, I think there might be a date which, in the photocopy, is obscured by --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "From Kiseljak 2100 hours TACSAT 21 March."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I'm sorry to jump around like this, but at the bottom of the page is the entry that I'm interested in. You can see -- in fact just read out the entry.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "0800, 22 March, to Kiseljak. HF --" in other words by HF radio, not the TACSAT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Oh, right. The text that appears underneath is for the 22nd -- entries for the 22nd of --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- March. Thank you. I'm sorry. Now if you look at the entries, please, could you just read them out. As best you can.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Number 1, marker panels, two times Dayglo orange. Five foot by --" it's a dimension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- in T. "Number 2. Confirm secure COMMs team to arrive by helicopter. Yes. "3. Find out how many lying wounded, sitting wounded. Numbers changing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "4. Request Canada inform next-of-kin of armoured personnel carrier crew that they are doing a fantastic job and inform next-of-kin that they are safe and sound."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "5. Oric said he received message from --" and I turn to the next page -- "Halilovic to suspend all hostile actions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That entry there is what I'm interested in. What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a reference to General Morillon telling me later on the previous day that Colonel Oric had, when the prisoners of war were being handed over, told him that Halilovic had ordered him to suspend all hostile actions. The reason for this was that Morillon had been pressing Oric to confirm that he had been ordered specifically by Halilovic to suspend all hostile actions because Dr. Ganic had told him that he had issued such instructions to Halilovic, to issue such instructions to Colonel Oric, but he wanted to confirm that that had actually happened. But I had not myself heard Colonel Oric say that. It was something that had occurred between General Morillon and Colonel Oric the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had heard words to the same effect previously on or around the 17th?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it wasn't specific. And the Serbs had been telling us that a public retraction of Halilovic's order to all Bosniaks to continue attacking towards eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina and Srebrenica and Gorazde, that public retraction had not yet happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. Thank you. The next day, the 23rd of March, did you see Mr. -- sorry, Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw him again in the evening. I would say the evening, but may I refer to my diary?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you unable to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You so may. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it's -- I may be able to assist you, if it's of any help to you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 35 -- we start with 23rd of March on page 3548.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did meet again once more with Colonel Oric on the 23rd of March, in the morning. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that His Honour is indeed correct, that the entries for the 23rd of March do start at 344 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3548. MR. DI FAZIO: 3548. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3548? Let me check. Yes. Sir, you are correct. They start on 3548. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. All right. Thanks. And if you would turn over to 3550 and you -- there is an entry there about a third of the way down, what I think is the 23rd of March. Can you just read that text out, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text says: "23 March, 10.40, Naser Oric. Commander tried to calm situation and prevent acts of desperation by local military and said he would go to Bratunac to try to gain cease-fire in south-east."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber how the encounter with Colonel Oric took place on that day.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a short meeting. Colonel Oric came into the PTT building and General Morillon was about to depart to go to Zvornik. And Colonel Oric was not feeling very well and was very depressed again, and General Morillon's main concern was to try and calm Colonel Oric so that he would not carry out any kind of attacks or offensive operations which would antagonise the Serbs and give the Serbs excuses to continue with their offensive because in previous meetings that we had had with the Serbs in Bratunac and down at the yellow bridge, we had, on a number of occasions, been told by the Serb military with whom we were meeting that attacks by the Bosniaks inside the Srebrenica enclave had continued. And each day we met the Serb colonel at the yellow bridge that told us three men were killed here, five men were killed there. These Muslims -- and that's the words he used -- do not want a cease-fire. They only want one when it suits them. And they were very angry. And very bitter. And were accusing us, United Nations, of being partisan. So what General Morillon was trying to do in this short meeting with Colonel Oric was to dissuade him from continuing with attacks which it would appear, from what the Serbs were telling us, were continuing, despite us having been told that he had received orders not to and despite his assurances to General Morillon that he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the time that you were in Srebrenica enclave, did you ever have occasion to go to a place called Zelina or Zelina Jadar and another place called Osmace?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Zelina Jadar, but not to Osmace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if those places were mentioned or raised during this encounter with Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may well have been. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's five minutes to go to the break. Could I seek your indulgence and ask for an early five minute adjournment? I am - I've made good ground this afternoon. I'm about to move on to some other topics that I may not need to go into and I would just like to consider my position. It will save time in the long run, if five minutes is not going to hurt us, and I'm pretty confident that I will be finishing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. We will have a -- I was going to suggest that we try and have a shorter break, 20 minutes instead of the usual 25 or 30 minutes, if that is -- MR. DI FAZIO: I just need to look at my notes, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we will have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had been -- you're not going to need your diary for what I have, the few remaining questions that I have, Colonel Tucker. Other than -- sorry. Let me start again. You've testified, just before the break, of your encounter with Colonel Oric on the 23rd of March, 1993. When did you eventually leave the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the -- I left the Srebrenica enclave for the last time on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you left the territory of the former Yugoslavia very shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two days later. Thank you. In between the 23rd of March and the 28th when you left Srebrenica, did you see Mr. Oric again?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the 23rd the -- of March 1993 in fact the last occasion you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I saw him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Colonel Tucker, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, in all fairness, I need to ask you, Mr. Jones, whether you are in a position to start the cross-examination straight away, or whether you want an adjournment now, especially since we also moved the sitting -- tomorrow's sitting from the afternoon to the morning, whether you want an adjournment now. It's up to you. We will accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I would be happy to start now, to make use of the time, and I did -- I was alerted by Mr. Di Fazio that he would finish fairly shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours would just give me a moment to get the lectern on the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, or good evening, Colonel Tucker. I'm just going to ask some preliminary questions and then go to your diary again, and I will be going through that basically from the start and asking for clarifications of certain entries. Firstly, very firstly, just to flesh out some more personal details: Your background is somewhat unusual, isn't it? You were in fact born in Kenya and educated in Belgium and Germany; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are your parents both British?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father is South African and my mother is Scottish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So English is your first language, obviously.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're currently a consultant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm currently a senior executive of a company, I was a consultant up until a couple of years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the nature of the business that that company conducts?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My current company is a supply chain management company. It's a company called Excel, which is the largest supply chain management company in the world. It's a FTSE 100 listed company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And your military training is as an artillery officer, as a gunner, as I think we say.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your training isn't as an intelligence officer, is it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did undergo some intelligence training. I spent a tour of duty in Northern Ireland as an intelligence officer early on in my career and went on about three months worth of courses about intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about sources of intelligence when you were in Bosnia. Is it right that those sources were briefing -- when they were doing it face-to-face, briefing General Morillon as opposed to you personally; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it was briefing General Morillon and I was present, though in a number of circumstances -- a number of situations when there was something that we needed to know more about or General Morillon had asked me to find me more about, I would then go and specifically ask for specific briefings about materials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I pause occasionally it is for the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You hear the interpreters. It is important --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is important to allow an interval between question and answer, because otherwise we will have problems. Please remember that interpreters are translating simultaneously into French and into Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally just on this subject, is it right that most of your communications with General Morillon were conducted in French?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you do have a copy of your diary, don't you, in front of you and also the photocopy so you can follow the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to start by asking you some questions about this diary. I think, though it's been done to a certain extent, what might be useful firstly is if we just establish the starting points for each date, each entry date. So would it be correct that the 10th of March starts on -- I will just do the four last numbers -- 3420?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just on that, you have no diary then of the period prior to that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is a different document, which I don't actually have with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You possess --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I do possess it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall roughly when that -- what period that covers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That diary covers from the day that I deployed into Srebrenica -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1992 and it goes up to the 9th of March, in other words the day before this document, and it picks up again for the last couple of days that I was in Bosnia before I departed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact is it right that that diary covers the period that you were in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carrying on with -- we may come back to that, but carrying on with the dates. 11th of March starts on 3429. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 12th of March, 3435?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 13th of March, 3442?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 14th of March, 3450?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the 15th of March, 3463?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the way, I think, just to make it clear, the objective of this exercise is that in due course we will be able to identify chronologically entries by these numbers. I apologise if this is a bit slow. 16th of March, 3480?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 17th of March, 3491?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the 18th of March is perhaps slightly more complicated, in that I think you'll agree there's an entry at 3502 of 18th of March and then also your evidence was it starts at 3504, so perhaps you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reference on 3502 is about the time that my next radio communication will be the next day. The 18th of March actually starts on 3504.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you for that. 19th of March, 3517. I should say halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of March? That's what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was actually asking about the 19th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's asking about the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right that starts on 3517, and I believe it would be highlighted in blue halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the... No. The 19th of March starts on the previous page, 3516.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at the top it says 1900 -- it says, where my finger is pointing - I'm looking at the ELMO - it says 1900, 19th of March, chief of staff and commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your first entry on that day started at 1900, or what is timed as 1900?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then the 20th of March, 3518; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 21st of March --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. 3517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Exactly. I would redirect the witness to page 3517, because I think it makes more sense if the first entry for the 20th is the one we see on halfway down page 3517 rather than 3518.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is 3517, as you say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Obviously we can't see on our copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I agree. I mean mine is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 21st of March, 3524, more than halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more days to go. 22nd of March, is that at 3540?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 23rd March, 3548?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 24th March, 3553?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I may stop the exercise there partly because I'm -- I've been unable to find the 25th of March. I don't know if you can help us with that. If you can, then please do let us know.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It goes straight to the meeting that we had with Milosevic in Belgrade, which starts on page 3558.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what page should that be, the meeting in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the 26th of March, does that start on 3563, or 3564?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. 26th of March starts on 3563. At the top of the page it says 26th March, 1993, Belgrade French embassy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. There are obviously a couple of more dates after that, but for my purposes, that's sufficient. One thing, the diary which you have, the original, it actually goes beyond the 28th of March, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we have is up to the 28th of March and then some pages from the back of your diary. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last entries in the diary are the -- about the meeting that General Morillon had with Lukic in Pale on his way from Srebrenica back to -- back to Sarajevo. It was with Lukic, Colonel Tolimir and General Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn right back to the beginning, and it's the second page in the copy, 3417 -- we need to look at the original as well. Isn't it right that that actually is a Post-it which has been stuck there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when that Post-it was placed there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three or four years ago.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall why you put a Post-it there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was trying to work out in my own mind exactly the exercise we have just been through, to sort out what actually happened when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not contemporaneous?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not contemporaneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also right -- if you look at the 21 March entry where you put Tuzla, and then you have 22nd of March, and you have an entry there about the funeral, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The line in between, "Released wounded prisoner" --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that was added after you had written the two other entries that I've just mentioned? It seems to have been squeezed in between the two.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to take you to certain pages of the diary. And if we could go first to 3426. I will just state for the record each

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. If you could now turn to page 3433. This is 11th of March. It refers to a meeting with the president of the war committee. Now firstly, as a general point, you knew of the war committee during your time in Srebrenica, didn't you? You didn't know of a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The translator for most of this was Mihailov and the words that he used in French were "committee."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you who all the members were of the war committee, you wouldn't be able to tell me, would you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be able to tell you a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe just to recapitulate on your testimony; Avdic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bektic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Senad Alic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at 3439 of your diary.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Senad Alic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Mukanovic, who we've discussed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the brother of Murat Effendic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these are five people, and as far as you're concerned, those were all members of the war committee?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there may have been other members?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly others who were represented as members, but I never found out what their names were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you've referred to meetings with or discussions with the war committee, you were referring to a meeting with at least Avdic.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe with one or two other people present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes as many as seven or eight. Sometimes literally only two or three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes literally only Avdic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a couple of times just Avdic, but I would not have described a meeting with Avdic alone as being a meeting with the war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With one or two other people for it to be a committee?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this has emerged from your testimony, but it's right, isn't it, that you didn't see Naser Oric in Srebrenica until the 17th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I saw him on four occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned how the war committee were sending messages to Oric to come to Srebrenica. Were you aware that he was very busy fighting the Serb offensive that was going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was what we were firstly told by the war committee and, secondly, it made obvious sense. He had a job to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could understand perhaps that he wasn't avoiding you, but that he had, as you say, other things to do?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not believe that he was avoiding us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 3434, please. Again, this is the 11th of March. I would like you just to read the section where you have a name written between two lines and I suggest to you that that is Von Recklinghausen?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just read those three lines.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Von Recklinghausen said that more than a thousand shells had hit KP --" Konjevic Polje -- "after Morillon left and that between 100 and 200 had been killed. He, Philip Von Recklinghausen, saw bodies and that there were now more than 500 injured."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Von Recklinghausen was a German photographer who was in Srebrenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was in Srebrenica when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware, aren't you, from Major Alan Abraham and the British soldiers who stayed behind in Konjevic Polje, that there was indeed a terrible shelling in Konjevic Polje after Morillon left?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time, we didn't know. We only met again with Major Abraham about the 24th of March. We had no communications with the British convoy which had gone back into Konjevic Polje at the same time as General Morillon went into Srebrenica. This British convoy went into try and evacuate the injured. We had no communications with them because we did not have the right type of radio sets to be able to communicate with the British armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You subsequently learned?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And wasn't that shelling, in fact, the subject of Cheshire sitreps?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also read General Morillon's book, Croire et Oser about his experiences in Sarajevo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He too refers to the shelling of Konjevic Polje, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it's a long time since I read it, but I'm pretty sure he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's actually an exhibit but I will come to that I think tomorrow. It might be easier logistically. And you understood, didn't you, when you were blocked in Srebrenica, that this fear that the same thing would happen in Konjevic Polje is very much what was motivating the people to try and keep you there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware when you were dealing with the people who were blocking you that many of them were from Cerska and Konjevic Polje who had been displaced to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were afraid they were going to get shelled again?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their belief and their concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you go back to 3439, which we saw earlier because it had the names of the -- who you say were in the war committee. It's actually the bottom half I want to ask you about now. This is 12th of March, 1993. And you have reference to Jagodnja and Joseva. Could you read those few lines and explain what that is about.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Jagodnja and Joseva, north, north-west of Skelani, an attack from Fakovici and that they were taken today, 12 March, by the Serbs. That is something which I was told by a member of the war committee at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to summarise, that would refer on the 12th of March to a Serb attack from Fakovici on those two places which are located north, north-west of Skelani and they were in fact taken by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I believe. I do not personally know Jagodnja or Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move now to page 3442. This would be the 13th of March. There is mention again to one of those locations. And I will have a stab at reading what's written there. "1. Reported attacks with helicopters on Jagodnja in Miholjevine refugees flooding into Srebrenica from all directions. Situation could get tough." I'm moving down to the second paragraph -- second sentence of paragraph 4: "Local commander appears helpless." And then, "5. Maybe Naser Oric could help." Is that correct, firstly, reading --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where we see "attacks with helicopters," was it your understanding that would be Serb helicopters?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact the word "Serb" is between the word "reported" and "attacks."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. "Reported Serb attacks with helicopters."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the information that refugees were flooding into Srebrenica, from all directions was presumably something you saw yourself. Or is that secondhand information?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is information -- we could see that ourselves. That's what General Morillon had seen in the previous night whilst he was in that destroyed building watching it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sentence paragraph 5 "Maybe Naser Oric could help," isn't that expression of your opinion or whoever provided this information, that he could maybe help with the problems you had with the women's committee?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you certainly didn't consider that he was behind what the women's committee was doing at that stage?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you say "local commander appears helpless," that obviously refers to someone other than Naser Oric, does it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was the Srebrenica war committee and the military people who attended that committee meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it local commander or local commanders? Perhaps I'm misreading it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- written there is "local commander," in the singular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware of local military commanders in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving forward to 3446. For the record, this is 13th of March. If you could read paragraphs 3 and 4 on that page.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 reads: "Hundreds of refugees are streaming into Srebrenica. A potential disaster is in the making. All diplomatic pressure should be brought to bear to halt the Serbs." Then number 4: "Commander believes Serb military are going far beyond the directions given by their politicians."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. A general question and I may be skipping ahead to something, but you've referred to -- well, this clearly refers to offensives which were going on by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also spoken of attempts by General Morillon to have Colonel Oric, as you referred to him, stop his offensives. Was it really your understanding that there were two sets of offensives going on? Or was this diplomatic peacekeeper language to try to have a solution?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What -- the Serb offensive is what I would describe as an offensive in major areas. What Colonel Oric was doing, our understanding was, was selected individual attacks. In other words, raids. Not an offensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you don't know any locations of any of those alleged raids?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have -- we had no information at all. We only had what the Serbs had, in a couple of occasions, alleged and -- but we had no personal knowledge of anything specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, and in fact the Serbs throughout the conflict in Bosnia and during the time you were in Srebrenica continually used as a pretext for prosecuting their war aim, the excuse that Muslims were launching raids or provocations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That excuse was used by all three factions all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you took -- you took it with a very large pinch of salt, I take it.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed that in the current circumstances in Srebrenica it was highly likely that Colonel Oric was carrying out raids. It's what we would have done in his position. Whether he was carrying out attacks against civilian populations and killing civilians or massacring civilians we had no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the next page, 3447, and I think it's correct to say that that -- the note at the bottom, where an arrow leads to, is in fact coming from the previous page. You have the words "It's an emergency" and I will let you read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That writing is in fact General Morillon's handwriting. And he inserted it at the end of his statements, the one that he read out loud over the loudspeaker. And it says: "It's an emergency for the thousands of refugees. Many of them haven't got anything, got nothing to eat for five days."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said that, I take it he wasn't being hyperbolic, that was based on real information that he had?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can sit here and say yes, I saw that. It is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that theme, did you not see people in Srebrenica who were in extremely emaciated state? I'm not talking about the Serb prisoner you mentioned, but Muslims who were in an extremely emaciated state?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you can just turn to the next page, 3448, please. And I wonder if I could ask you to read paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 on that page.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read the sentence above it, which is in the highlighter which is difficult to see. It says: "UNMO patrol reported --" our UN military observer patrol reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is items 1, 2, and 3. Item 1 is "Village Osmace grid, Charlie Pepper under constant attack by tanks firing in indirect role from grid Charlie Pepper 7474 and by artillery and multiple rocket-launchers. Village severely beaten up. Later fire, ten rounds per hour."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If I could stop you there. Just for clarity's sake: The tanks, the artillery, the multiple rocket-launchers --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were all Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "2. At 1715 hours, saw one propeller driven biplane drop three bombs on village Gladovici, grid Charlie Pepper 7173 and fly over Drina into Serbia. Thereafter two single engine propeller driven monoplanes came from Serbia, circled, dropped some bombs, and flew away over Serbia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I would ask you to pause there for a moment. This is information from the UNMOs. Is it something you also observed, Serb airplanes over Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not, but the UNMOs told me they did and this is part of their report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it right that actually the diplomatic state of play at the time, it was very serious for Serb planes from Serbia proper to be involved because that was in violation of various UN resolutions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This particular report went all the way to New York because this was the first clear evidence that existed in the international community that Serbia itself was engaged in military operations inside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. An then the third paragraph and the concluding paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "3. Non-stop streams of refugees from these and other outlying villages heading for Srebrenica. This info must be passed immediately to Zagreb for New York as is first independent confirmation of aircraft attacking from Serbia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we can move forward to 3550. And you've been asked about the jamming of the communications already by His Honour. It does, however, lead into the subject of the radio communications obliquely and so I will take this opportunity to ask you a little about that. You described the radio setup which you saw in the PTT as being sophisticated. You've pointed to the size of the equipment, the fact that it had a lot of knobs and switches and the use of headphones as indices of sophistication. I put it to you that in fact that's not a particularly sophisticated analysis, is it, of whether or not the equipment is sophisticated. Firstly, large equipment could be very unsophisticated. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, would Your Honours give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, would you agree that communications from the radio could be intercepted by the Serbs, it was an open line?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As a military man you know, I suppose, that it's next to useless to give military commands over a line that the enemy can listen to. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the only means you have, you take that risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what frequency the -- they were using?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many watts the radio was generated by? How many --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't have been much, because they only had a very faint, very weak electricity supply, and I believe that they had a bank of batteries and they had to charge up the batteries before they could actually use the transmitter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree it could be about fifty watts?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be surprised if it was as much as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "powerful," you're not speaking in terms of wattage, are you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm speaking in terms of reliability and solidity of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It's a subject I may come back to, but thank you for those answers. Now, if we move ahead to 3453. This would be the 14th of March. I would ask if you could just read into the record the second paragraph of that sitrep dealing with the humanitarian situation on the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "2. Humanitarian situation. "A. Claims of 60.000 to 80.000 in Srebrenica pocket would appear exaggerated. Population fleeing to Srebrenica from all directions at 500 to 1.000 people per day. "B. Hundreds of refugees camping out in streets of Srebrenica require UNHCR plastic sheeting in large quantities. "C. Thousands of refugees in town and vicinity. "D. 130 lying wounded in hospital, estimated another 60 to 80 in surrounding area." Then with a line through it, it says "Remainder of wounded are walking. Numbers going up by two or three. Antibiotics are top priority."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you move on to the next page, describe the temperature at this time as being minus 15 to minus 20 degrees Centigrade.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th it had started getting quite a lot warmer, but it was still down 10, minus 15 at nights. In the sun, in the day, it would probably break zero, but it was still damn cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people you saw on the streets burning plastic crates when you first arrived were in a pretty desperate situation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in a terrible state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next page, 3454, and read (B) there, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not connect to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could tell us what it connects to.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It connects to the next page in -- if you look at page 35 -- 3455 you have: "1. One combat activities, 1a. Srebrenica relatively quiet." B. crossed out and there is a line which then goes across. In the diary, the line goes across to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you could read that with the -- with our understanding that it in fact goes from 3455 and it's a sitrep from the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "B. Serb attacks and bombing as reported yesterday by UNMOs. Correction to last night's report. First aircraft dropped three bombs on Gladovici. Second aircraft dropped three bombs on same village. Third aircraft dropped three bombs on Osatica" and a grid reference. "Second and third aircraft believed to be Kraguj bombers. Local commander said they flew from Ponikve --" I'm sorry, my pronunciation is bad -- "airfield in Serbia." Then crossed out: "15 kilometres at a bearing of 2300 Mls from Bajina Basta."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was information provided by the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
